opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Gloria, thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, and we don't work for any company, union or party. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ay, of course, honey. Sit down. I've got a colour processing, so I'm all yours for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, so what? Nobody's getting their hair cut by a search engine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. My clients are my friends. Some of them have been with me twenty years. A computer can't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Maybe use AI for the booking texts and the Instagram captions. My daughter already does that for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Happy. Nothing to worry about.

S0.say: So what? Nobody's getting their hair cut by a search engine.
S0.think: Nothing changes; her clients are friends of twenty years.
S0.do: Keeps going as now and lets her daughter use AI for booking texts and captions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the girls coming up should learn a trade with their hands. That's what I tell my nieces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's still nothing. If anything, more young people might come to beauty school because office jobs are harder to get. I could hire good people more easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe take on an apprentice. Keep building the colour work, that's where the money is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, even.

S1.say: Young women should learn a trade with their hands.
S1.think: Nothing changes, and harder office hiring might send good young people to beauty school.
S1.do: Takes on an apprentice and builds her colour work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for those families. In the chair, I'd listen. People tell their stylist everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few clients might stretch their appointments, six weeks to eight. That's normal when times are hard. I've been through recessions. People still want to feel nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said six weeks to eight. Have you seen that happen before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh yes. Every time the economy dips. It comes back. My regulars always come back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. Maybe a little cheaper option for a trim, so I don't lose anyone. Keep my savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Sad for my clients, but okay.

S2.say: It's a shame for those families. In the chair, I'd listen; people tell their stylist everything.
S2.think: Some clients would stretch appointments, but she's seen recessions and people still want to feel nice.
S2.do: Adds a cheaper trim option and keeps her savings untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need jobs, not handouts. Somebody has to make sure regular people get a piece of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is fine, I'm sure of it. But my two are teenagers. One wants to be a lawyer. If lawyers are losing jobs to computers, what do I tell her? That's what keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to my kids about what they want to study, honestly. Maybe tell the older one to get a licence in something hands-on too, as a backup. In the salon, same as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Not for me, for my kids.

S3.say: Families need jobs, not handouts. Regular people need a piece of this.
S3.think: Her job is fine, but her teenager wants to be a lawyer, and that path now looks shaky.
S3.do: Talks honestly with her teens about study plans and suggests a hands-on licence as backup.
S3.feel: A little uneasy, for her kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in care homes? That's sad. Old people need a hand on their shoulder. Same as my clients need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still don't see a robot doing a balayage, or listening to a woman cry about her divorce. I really don't. But my clients who work in warehouses and kitchens, they'd be hurting. Fewer appointments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my prices fair, keep my regulars, put a bit more away. Maybe tell my kids the hands-on backup isn't so safe after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm okay, but everyone around me isn't.

S4.say: Robots in care homes is sad. Old people need a hand on their shoulder, like my clients need me.
S4.think: No robot will do a balayage or listen to a divorce story, but clients in warehouses and kitchens would cut back.
S4.do: Keeps prices fair, holds on to regulars, saves more, and rethinks the hands-on backup advice for her kids.
S4.feel: Uneasy: she's okay, but those around her aren't.
